title: The lake Seattle saved
teaches: Edmondson, sewage and a lake that cleared

blocks.text: In 1955 a University of Washington zoologist named W. Thomas Edmondson, who studied the tiny animals of lakes, found something new in the water samples he took from Lake Washington, Seattle's big lake on its eastern edge. It was *Oscillatoria rubescens*, a cyanobacterium that forms reddish scums and is a well-known sign, in the lakes of Europe, of water overfed with nutrients. It had never been recorded in the lake before.

Edmondson knew what it meant. Since 1941 the growing towns around the lake had built sewage treatment plants that discharged their treated water into it, eleven of them by the 1950s. Treatment removed the solids and germs, but not the dissolved nutrients, above all phosphorus. Lesson 13 showed what that does to a lake. Within a few years the water had turned green and murky in summer, and drifts of algae rotted on the beaches.

Edmondson spent the late 1950s measuring the lake: its phosphorus, its algae, its oxygen, and how clear it was, using a **Secchi disk**, a white plate lowered on a rope until it vanishes from sight[^secchi]. He wrote articles and gave talks to clubs and councils explaining that the algae were being fed by the phosphorus in the sewage, and that the lake could be saved only if the sewage went somewhere else.

This was before the Lake 226 experiment of lesson 13, in which phosphorus alone turned half a lake green, and many people thought nitrogen or carbon might be to blame, or that the lake was simply ageing. Edmondson's measurements showed the algae tracking the phosphorus[^nutrients]. A citizens' campaign led by the lawyer James Ellis proposed a new regional agency, Metro, to collect the sewage around the lake and pipe it, after treatment, into the deep, fast-flushed waters of Puget Sound. Voters rejected the plan in March 1958, then approved a smaller version in September[^metro].

Metro built the pipes and plants, and between 1963 and 1968 the sewage was diverted from the lake. The lake's water is replaced by its rivers in about three years, so the phosphorus washed out quickly. The algae fell with it, and by the early 1970s the Secchi disk, which had disappeared about a metre down at the worst, could be seen three metres down or more. Edmondson had predicted the recovery, and it came about as he said.

Then, in 1976, the lake cleared further, and nobody had predicted that. The water flea *Daphnia*, a grazer of algae, suddenly became abundant. Edmondson and his colleagues worked out why: a small shrimp-like predator, *Neomysis*, which had kept the *Daphnia* down, had declined as the longfin smelt that eat it increased. With *Daphnia* grazing hard, the algae fell further and summer clarity reached six metres or more. Lesson 8's cascade had happened in a lake: fish to shrimp to water flea to algae.

blocks.task: Divert the sewage, then bring back the Daphnia

blocks.text: Lake Washington's recovery was one of the first times a polluted lake had been cleaned by deciding to, and the evidence was clear because Edmondson had measured it all before, during and after. His papers, and the Lake 226 experiment soon after, helped persuade governments in North America and Europe to limit phosphorus in sewage and in washing powders in the 1970s. Lake Erie, which was choking on algae in the 1960s, improved as phosphorus was cut[^erie].

The lake today faces newer problems. It is warmer than it was, which favours some algae and stresses cold-water fish. Its salmon, the sockeye and chinook that pass through to the Cedar River and Issaquah Creek, face predators that thrive in warm, clear water. But it is still the lake that people swim in on a summer day in Seattle, and that, in 1958, was not a safe bet.

blocks.title: Outside
points: Make a Secchi disk from a white plastic lid about 20 centimetres across, a weight and a marked cord. From a dock on a calm day, lower it in the shade until it vanishes, raise it until it reappears, and average the two depths. Try it on the same lake in spring and late summer.

blocks.caption: Five questions on Lake Washington
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What did Edmondson find in Lake Washington in 1955?
choices: A cyanobacterium known as a sign of overfed lakes
A fish that had never been seen there
items.why: Oscillatoria rubescens had warned of over-fertilised lakes in Europe.

items.ask: Where was the lake's extra phosphorus coming from?
choices: Treated sewage from plants discharging into the lake
Silt from logging around the lake
items.why: Treatment removed solids and germs but not dissolved phosphorus.

items.ask: Why did the lake clear within a few years of the diversion?
choices: Its water is replaced in about three years, so the phosphorus washed out
items.why: With the sewage gone, the rivers flushed the phosphorus out and the algae fell with it.

items.ask: Why did the lake clear further in 1976?
choices: Daphnia became abundant and grazed the algae down
A cold winter killed the algae
items.why: The predator that had kept Daphnia down declined. A cascade, as in lesson 8.

items.ask: A Secchi disk vanishes 1 metre down in one summer and 6 metres down in another. What changed?
choices: The water held far fewer algae in the second
The water was warmer in the second
The disk was lowered faster in the first
items.why: The disk shows how clear the water is, and in a lake like this the algae decide that.

summary: **In 1955 Edmondson found a warning alga in Lake Washington.** Treated sewage was feeding the lake phosphorus.
**He argued that the sewage had to go.** His measurements showed the algae tracking the phosphorus.
**Voters approved a smaller Metro plan in September 1958.** Sewage was diverted to Puget Sound between 1963 and 1968.
**The lake cleared in a few years.** Its water is replaced in about three, and the phosphorus washed out.
**In 1976 Daphnia cleared it further.** A cascade from fish to shrimp to water flea to algae.
**The recovery helped persuade governments to limit phosphorus.** Lake Erie improved too.

secchi.title: The Secchi disk
secchi.text: Angelo Secchi, an Italian astronomer, used white disks to measure the clearness of the Mediterranean in 1865 for the Papal Navy. The method is so simple and consistent that volunteers' readings over decades are used in scientific studies of lakes.

metro.title: Why the second vote passed
metro.text: The March 1958 plan covered sewage, transport, water and parks across a wide area, and lost in the suburbs. The September plan covered only sewage in a smaller area. Ellis went on to lead the Forward Thrust campaign of the late 1960s, which paid for parks and the Kingdome.

erie.title: Lake Erie again
erie.text: Lake Erie improved through the 1970s and 1980s, but blooms returned in the 2000s, fed by phosphorus washing off farmland after storms. In 2014 toxins from a bloom shut off Toledo's drinking water for two days.

nutrients.title: Why not nitrogen
nutrients.text: Edmondson noticed that the ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus in the lake suggested phosphorus was the nutrient that ran short first. Schindler's Lake 226 later showed the same thing directly, by adding nitrogen and carbon to one half of a lake and phosphorus too to the other. Only the phosphorus half bloomed.
